description: Test your knowledge of the gluteal region and back of thigh anatomy, covering gluteal muscles, the sciatic nerve, hamstrings, and clinical correlations for MBBS anatomy.

cards.text: What are the origin and insertion points of gluteus maximus?
cards.answer: Origin: ilium (posterior gluteal line), sacrum, coccyx, and sacrotuberous ligament. Insertion: iliotibial tract (upper 3/4) and gluteal tuberosity of femur (lower 1/4).

tip.tip: IT band takes the majority; only lower quarter attaches to femur

cards.text: Why is weakness of gluteus medius and minimus clinically significant?
cards.answer: These muscles abduct the hip and stabilize the pelvis during single-leg standing. Weakness causes Trendelenburg sign—the pelvis tilts toward the non-weight-bearing side.

tip.tip: "One leg standing = medius/minimus working" — classic gait assessment

cards.text: Name the six deep lateral rotators using the mnemonic.
cards.answer: Piriformis, Obturator internus, Gemellus superior, Gemellus inferior, Quadratus femoris. Mnemonic: POGO-Q or "Piece Of Outgoing Internal Girls Quietly."

tip.tip: All insert on greater trochanter; all laterally rotate the extended hip

cards.text: From which spinal nerve roots does the sciatic nerve form and where does it exit?
cards.answer: Forms from L4, L5, S1, S2, S3. Exits through the greater sciatic foramen, typically below the piriformis muscle.

cards.text: What is the preferred safe zone for gluteal intramuscular injection?
cards.answer: Upper outer quadrant of gluteus maximus or ventrogluteal site (over gluteus medius/minimus at greater trochanter). Avoid lower inner quadrant—risk of sciatic nerve damage.

tip.tip: "Upper outer = safe; lower inner = sciatic danger"

cards.text: List the three hamstring muscles and their primary hip and knee actions.
cards.answer: Biceps femoris, semitendinosus, and semimembranosus. All three flex the knee and extend the hip.

tip.tip: Biceps (two heads); Semis (two S-muscles) — all "hamstrings" on posterolateral thigh

cards.text: Into which two nerves does the sciatic nerve divide and where does this occur?
cards.answer: Divides into common peroneal (fibular) and tibial nerves, typically at the apex of the popliteal fossa.

tip.tip: Sciatic splits at the back of the knee into common peroneal and tibial

cards.text: What is piriformis syndrome and who is at highest risk?
cards.answer: Sciatic nerve irritation caused by piriformis muscle spasm. Most common in individuals whose sciatic nerve passes through (not below) piriformis, especially with prolonged sitting.

tip.tip: Sitting too long + nerve through muscle = pain; classic in long-distance drivers and cyclists
